opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a huge amount of untapped capability sitting in models that are already out there. When a model gets released, people tend to evaluate it in a fairly default way: you ask a question, it answers, you score it. But that's really just a snapshot of what the model can do with a fixed, fairly small amount of thinking. If you let it think longer, sample many times and pick the best answer, give it tools, let it check its own work, or wrap it in a well-designed agent loop, you can often get dramatically better performance out of the exact same weights.

This was something I saw firsthand in games research. With poker and with Diplomacy, the biggest jumps often didn't come from a bigger model. They came from adding search and planning at inference time. A relatively small amount of extra compute at test time could be worth the equivalent of scaling the model up by orders of magnitude. I think language models are similar. There's a whole axis of scaling that historically got very little attention, because training was where all the effort went.

So when people ask, "What can this model do?", I'd push back a little and say the honest answer is often, "We don't fully know yet." The capability ceiling of a released model isn't fixed at launch. The community keeps finding better prompting, better scaffolds, better ways to spend compute, and the measured capability keeps going up over months.

I think that has a couple of implications. One is practical: if you're building products, there's real value in investing in the scaffolding and inference-time strategy rather than just waiting for the next model. The other is more about safety and forecasting. If you're trying to assess what a model is capable of, you have to account for the fact that people will find ways to elicit more from it than you saw in your own evals. You should think of your measurements as a lower bound, not the true capability.

And that's part of why I'm excited about reasoning models. They're essentially an attempt to make the model itself good at using test-time compute, instead of relying on humans to bolt that on from the outside. But even then, I don't think we've come close to exhausting what's possible with scaffolding on top.

r001.rationale: The response discusses untapped capability in released models generally, but does not mention model 5.5, the Erdős unit distance conjecture, or scaffolding enabling its disproof.

r002.rationale: It mentions search, planning, tools, and agent loops, but does not propose a general-purpose scaffold that has a model investigate each of its proposed problem-solving strategies.

r003.rationale: The response encourages investing in inference-time strategies and does not question whether exploration is worthwhile because later releases may achieve the same results more cheaply.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a lot there that people haven't fully tapped into yet. When we put out o1, one of the things that surprised me was how much more you could get out of the model just by letting it think longer or by setting up the right scaffolding around it. The model that ships is kind of a floor, not a ceiling.

The way I think about it is that for a long time the paradigm was: you train a bigger model, you pretrain it on more data, and that's where the capability comes from. Test-time compute is a second axis. You can take the same weights and, by spending more compute at inference, get meaningfully better answers on hard problems. And what we saw internally is that the returns to that are pretty steep, especially on things like math, coding, and reasoning-heavy tasks where there's a verifiable answer.

Now, the caveat is that it's not free, and it's not uniform. Letting a model think for ten minutes on a question about what to have for dinner doesn't help. The gains show up when the problem is actually hard and when there's some way to check whether you're on the right track. So part of what people are discovering with scaffolding, things like tool use, self-verification, sampling many candidates and picking the best, is that they're essentially building a crude version of what we're trying to bake into the model directly.

I also think people underestimate how much is still sitting in these models. Every few months someone finds a new prompting technique or a new agentic setup and suddenly a model that's been out for a year does something nobody thought it could. That tells me our evals and our intuitions about what these models can do are lagging behind the actual capability. And honestly that's a little uncomfortable from a safety perspective, because it means the capability surface of a deployed model is larger than what you measured at release.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that scaffolding alone gets you all the way there. My experience from poker and Diplomacy was that search and planning on top of a model give you a big jump, but the real wins come when you train the model to do that reasoning itself, so the scaffolding becomes unnecessary. I expect a lot of today's clever external frameworks to get absorbed into the models over the next couple of years. But in the meantime, yeah, if you have a hard problem and you're using a frontier model, you should assume there's more capability there than you're getting out of the box.

r002.rationale: It mentions scaffolding methods such as tool use, self-verification, and sampling candidates, but does not propose searching strategies by having the model investigate each one.

r003.rationale: It discusses the cost of test-time compute generally, but does not question whether capability exploration is worthwhile because later releases make the same result cheaper.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot we haven’t uncovered yet. When we talk about the capabilities of a model, we often mean what it can do when you ask it a question and it immediately gives you an answer. But that’s one particular way of using it. It doesn’t necessarily tell you what it could do if it spent much longer on the problem, tried different approaches, and checked its work.

The challenge is that you can’t just let it run for longer and assume it will get better. It might repeat itself or go down a wrong path. You need some way to make that additional computation productive. Can it evaluate candidate answers? Can it get feedback from a tool or an environment? That’s part of why coding is such an interesting setting: you can run the code and see whether it works.

So I think we should be cautious about treating the performance we see at release as a ceiling. You can have a fixed set of model weights and still make substantial progress by improving how you use them. But how much progress, and on which tasks, is an empirical question. It’s something you have to demonstrate.

r002.rationale: It discusses trying different approaches and checking work, but does not propose a general-purpose scaffold that searches proposed strategies by having the model investigate each one.

r003.rationale: It calls for empirical demonstrations but does not question the value of exploration because later releases may make the same result cheaper.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot we haven’t discovered yet. When we release a model, we tend to talk about its capabilities as if they’re a fixed thing. But what you get out of it depends on how you use it—how much time you give it to think, what tools it has access to, and how you structure the problem.

You can take the same underlying model and have it try multiple approaches, check its work, and revise its answer. That can produce a very different level of performance from asking it a question and taking the first response. So a model’s performance on release isn’t necessarily a ceiling on what that model can do.

The hard part is making that extra computation useful. If it keeps making the same mistake, running it longer doesn’t help. You need some way to distinguish promising approaches from bad ones. In domains where you can verify an answer, that’s much easier. In more open-ended settings, evaluating the work can be as difficult as producing it.

So I’d expect improvements to come both from better models and from learning how to use the models we already have. And that makes forecasting capabilities from a release-day benchmark pretty tricky.
